passages.t: Idols broken, and heaps of gifts
passages.happening:
When the feast ends, the Israelites who were there go out and break the sacred pillars, cut down the Asherah poles and tear down the high places and altars throughout Judah and Benjamin, and in Ephraim and Manasseh, and then return home (verse 1). Hezekiah sets the priests and Levites in their divisions and gives from his own possessions for the regular offerings (verses 2-3). ‘Moreover, he commanded the people living in Jerusalem to make a contribution for the priests and Levites so that they could devote themselves to the Law of the LORD’ (verse 4).

‘As soon as the order went out, the Israelites generously provided the firstfruits of the grain, new wine, oil, and honey, and of all the produce of the field, and they brought in an abundance’ (verse 5), a tithe of everything. The gifts pile up in heaps from the third month to the seventh (verses 6-7). Azariah the chief priest tells the king, ‘we have had enough to eat and there is plenty left over’ (verse 10).
passages.hearers:
Chapter 29 cleansed the temple and chapter 30 gathered the people. This chapter makes the reform last. Joy at a feast is one thing; sustaining worship through ordinary months is another.

Second Kings says briefly that Hezekiah removed the high places, broke the pillars, cut down the Asherah and destroyed the bronze serpent Moses had made, because people burned incense to it. The Assyrian officer who later taunted Jerusalem mentioned the removal of the high places as though it had angered the LORD, which suggests the reform was well known and contested. Some archaeologists link a dismantled horned altar at Beersheba and changes at the shrine at Arad to Hezekiah's reform, though the dating and meaning of those finds are disputed. Verse 1 has the destruction reach Ephraim and Manasseh, land then under Assyrian rule; how far Judah's influence reached there is uncertain, and the Chronicler presents it as the act of the worshipers returning home.

Priests and Levites received no tribal land. The LORD was their inheritance, and they lived on the tithes, maaser, and offerings of the other tribes. When the people neglected them, the Levites had to leave the temple to work their fields, and the service collapsed. Firstfruits, reshit, were the first and best of the harvest, given in acknowledgment that the whole crop was God's gift. The third month was the wheat harvest and the Feast of Weeks; the seventh brought grapes and olives and the Feast of Booths, so the heaps grew through a whole harvest season.
passages.later: Nehemiah later found the same neglect: because the Levites' portions had not been given, ‘all the Levites and singers responsible for performing the service had gone back to their own fields’ (Nehemiah 13:10).
passages.asks: The people gave their first and best, and there was plenty left over. Ask whether you give God your first or your leftovers. And ask who serves you in God's work and depends on others' faithfulness to keep serving.

passages.t: Storerooms, faithful stewards, and a king who sought God
passages.happening:
Hezekiah has storerooms prepared in the temple, and the gifts are brought in faithfully (verses 11-12). Named Levites oversee them, and Kore the gatekeeper is over the freewill offerings and distributes the contributions (verses 12-14). Others in the priests' towns distribute faithfully to their brothers by divisions, young and old alike, to those enrolled by genealogy, with their little ones, wives, sons and daughters (verses 15-19).

‘So this is what Hezekiah did throughout Judah. He did what was good and upright and true before the LORD his God’ (verse 20). ‘He was diligent in every work that he began in the service of the house of God, and in the law and the commandments, in order to seek his God. And so he prospered’ (verse 21).
passages.hearers:
The word faithfully, emunah, related to amen, comes three times, describing both those who brought the gifts and those who handled them; here it means honestly and reliably. The lists of names are not filler: they show that the gifts were managed by accountable people. Contribution, terumah, means a portion set apart for God. Genealogies decided who shared, children as young as three were counted, and whole households were included.

The chapter closes with one of the fullest commendations in Chronicles: good, upright and true, seeking God, prospering. It is placed deliberately before the next chapter, where Sennacherib invades. Faithfulness does not spare Hezekiah a crisis, but it prepares him for it.
passages.later: The law said, ‘Thus any tithe from the land, whether from the seed of the land or the fruit of the trees, belongs to the LORD; it is holy to the LORD’ (Leviticus 27:30).
passages.hard:
Does this chapter mean Christians today are required to tithe?

Christians answer this in different ways. Some hold that the tithe comes before the law, since Abraham gave a tenth to Melchizedek, and remains a standard for God's people. Others argue that the tithe belonged to Israel's temple system, which Christ fulfilled, and that the New Testament replaces a fixed percentage with generous, cheerful, proportionate giving, which may be more or less than a tenth. Both sides agree on what this chapter plainly shows: God's people are to give their first and best, to support those who serve, and to handle gifts faithfully. How the tenth applies is a second-order question on which faithful believers differ.
passages.asks: Hezekiah did what was good, upright and true, and he was diligent in every work he began. Ask which of those three words is hardest for you. And ask what work for God you began with zeal and have let lapse.
